2027-05-06.title: The Ascension of our Lord

2027-05-06.alt: Sixth Thursday of Resurrection: THE ASCENSION OF OUR LORD, a Feast of Our Lord, an important feast and a day of obligation in the Syro-Malabar Church. Longer forms in the calendar: 2 Kings 2:1–15; Acts 1:1–14; 1 Timothy 1:18–2:15; Luke 24:36–53. St Dominic Savio (6 May) gives way. The Latin Church in India keeps the Ascension on Sunday 9 May; in the Latin calendar today is a weekday of Easter there (verify locally). The Queen of Heaven is still prayed until Pentecost.
2027-05-06.verse: While he was blessing them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven.
theo: Forty days after Easter the Church celebrates the Ascension of our Lord. The Acts of the Apostles tells us that after his suffering Jesus “presented himself alive to them by many convincing proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God” (Acts 1:3), and then, from the Mount of Olives, he was taken up. Our Syro-Malabar Church keeps this day on the Thursday, as the ancient Church did, as a Feast of our Lord and a day of obligation; in the Syriac tradition it is called Sullaqa, the going up. (The Latin Church in India celebrates it this year on Sunday 9 May.) What do we celebrate? Not that Jesus has left us. The Creed says: “He ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of the Father.” The same Jesus who was born of the Virgin Mary, who died and rose in his body, now enters with that body, glorified and bearing the wounds, into the glory of God. For the first time a human nature, our nature, is at the right hand of the Father. That is why the Church can sing on this day with joy rather than sadness. Where the Head has gone, the members hope to follow (Catechism 661). And from there, Peter will say at Pentecost, “Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you both see and hear” (Acts 2:33). The Ascension is the hinge between Easter and Pentecost.

The calendar opens the feast with a story from the Old Testament that the first Christians read as a prophecy of this day: the taking up of Elijah. The old prophet knows that the Lord is about to take him, and three times he tells his disciple Elisha to stay behind, at Gilgal, at Bethel, at Jericho. Three times Elisha answers, “As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.” At the Jordan Elijah strikes the water with his mantle and they cross on dry ground. Then the master asks, “Tell me what I may do for you, before I am taken from you.” Elisha asks a great thing: “Please let me inherit a double share of your spirit.” The answer is a condition: “if you see me as I am being taken from you, it will be granted you”. And then “a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them, and Elijah ascended in a whirlwind into heaven.” Elisha keeps watching and cries out, “Father, father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” Elisha saw, and so he received the spirit of his master; the mantle that fell from Elijah became his, and with it he struck the Jordan and it parted again. The disciples of Jesus are in Elisha's place. They watch their Master go up, and ten days later they will receive, not a double share of a prophet's spirit, but the Holy Spirit himself, the Spirit of the Son. Jesus had said it plainly: “it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16:7). The mantle of Christ is the Church's mission, and it has fallen on us.

In the Acts of the Apostles the disciples ask one last question: “Lord, is this the time when you will restore the kingdom to Israel?” Even after the Resurrection they are thinking of a kingdom like the kingdoms they knew. Jesus does not scold them; he redirects them: “It is not for you to know the times or periods that the Father has set by his own authority. But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.” The kingdom will come, but not by a calendar we can study; it will come through witnesses filled with the Spirit, moving outward from Jerusalem. One of those witnesses, Thomas, would carry the Gospel to the ends of the earth as Kerala then was. “When he had said this, as they were watching, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight.” In Scripture the cloud is the sign of God's presence: the cloud that led Israel in the desert, the cloud that filled the Temple, the cloud of the Transfiguration. Jesus is not travelling through space to a distant place; he is entering the presence of God, where he is near to every place. And then two men in white robes ask the question that the Church hears every year on this feast: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up toward heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.” The Ascension does not give us permission to stand staring at the sky. It sends us back to Jerusalem, to prayer, to the Spirit and to the work of witness, until he comes again.

The Epistle shows us what Christ does now at the right hand of the Father. “First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for everyone, for kings and all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and dignity.” Why should the Church pray for everyone, including rulers who may not know God? Because God “desires everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God; there is also one mediator between God and humankind, Christ Jesus, himself human, who gave himself a ransom for all”. Notice the words “himself human”. The one Mediator who has entered heaven is a man, our brother, who has not laid aside our nature. The Letter to the Hebrews says that “he entered into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24), and that “he always lives to make intercession” for those who approach God through him (Hebrews 7:25). When our Church prays in the Holy Qurbana for the Pope and the bishops, for rulers and for the whole world, for the sick and the departed, she prays with the ascended Christ and through him. Our prayers for the saints' intercession and for one another do not compete with his one mediation; they share in it, as members share in the life of the Head (Catechism 2634–2636).

Luke's Gospel ends with the same event told in a few unforgettable lines. Jesus opens their minds to understand the Scriptures: “Thus it is written, that the Messiah is to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins is to be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things.” He promises the gift of the Father: “so stay here in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high.” Then “he led them out as far as Bethany, and, lifting up his hands, he blessed them. While he was blessing them, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven.” The last image the apostles kept of Jesus on earth was of his raised, pierced hands, blessing them. Like a priest at the end of the Qurbana, he blesses and goes, and the blessing remains. And the disciples' response is surprising: “they worshiped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy; and they were continually in the temple blessing God.” Joy, not sorrow; worship, not loss. Acts adds that in the upper room they “were constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14). From tomorrow the Church enters these days of waiting with the Blessed Virgin Mary; many families and parishes pray a novena to the Holy Spirit, as Pope Leo XIII asked in 1897. Let us go up the mountain today with the apostles, receive his blessing, and come down with great joy to wait and pray for the Spirit.
conn: God has gone up with a shout.
“God has gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet” (Psalm 47:5): the Church sings this psalm on the Ascension.

“The Lord says to my lord, ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool’” (Psalm 110:1); “the Lord Jesus... was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:19).
Daniel saw “one like a human being coming with the clouds of heaven” and brought before the Ancient One (Daniel 7:13).
I go to prepare a place.
“If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, so that where I am, there you may be also” (John 14:3).
I am ascending to my Father.
To Mary Magdalene: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17).
“When he ascended on high he made captivity itself a captive; he gave gifts to his people” (Ephesians 4:8).
Stephen, dying, sees “the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!” (Acts 7:56).
Matthew's Gospel ends not with a departure but with a promise: “And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).
“So if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Colossians 3:1).
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the ascended Lord is not far away. He who is seated at the right hand of the Father comes down upon our altar in his Body and Blood, and lifts us up with him. St Leo the Great said that what was visible in our Redeemer has passed into the sacraments.
Luke's Gospel ends with Jesus lifting up his hands to bless his disciples. Every Qurbana ends with a blessing given in his name: the hands of the ascended Christ are still raised over his people.
Before the anaphora the priest invites us to lift up our minds on high. On this feast we understand why: our Head is there, and in the Qurbana heaven and earth are joined.

live: Take part in the Holy Qurbana today, a day of obligation, and make it a day of thanksgiving.
Begin tomorrow a novena to the Holy Spirit, with your family, together with Mary.
Pray today by name for those in authority, in the nation, the state, the Church and your workplace.
Tell one person this week what the risen and ascended Lord means to you.
Spend a few minutes tonight under the open sky, thanking Christ for preparing a place for you, then do one concrete act of service.
fathers: Christ is now exalted above the heavens, yet he still suffers on earth in his members, saying, Saul, why do you persecute me? While he is in heaven he is also with us; and we, while on earth, are with him. He did not leave heaven when he came down to us, and he has not left us when he went up again.

The Ascension of Christ is our own elevation; where the glory of the Head has gone, the hope of the body is called. What was visible in our Redeemer has passed over into the sacraments, so that faith might be more excellent and firm.

Our nature, which had been driven out of paradise and was unworthy even of the earth, today ascends above the angels and the cherubim and is seated on the royal throne. The Lord has taken up the first fruits of our race and presented them to the Father.
magis: The body of the risen Christ, after forty days, enters into the divine glory, symbolised by the cloud and by heaven, where he is seated at the right hand of God.
The Ascension marks the definitive entrance of Jesus' humanity into God's heavenly domain, from where he will come again; we have the hope of following him there.
Jesus Christ, the one priest of the new and eternal covenant, entered into heaven itself, where he permanently exercises his priesthood, for he always lives to make intercession for us.
Being seated at the right hand of the Father signifies the inauguration of the Messiah's kingdom, which will have no end.
Jesus Christ, having entered the sanctuary of heaven once and for all, intercedes constantly for us as the mediator who assures us of the permanent outpouring of the Holy Spirit.
Intercession is a prayer of petition which leads us to pray as Jesus did; he is the one intercessor with the Father on behalf of all.

2027-05-06.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, King of glory, today you ascended above the heavens and took our human nature to the right hand of the Father. As you blessed your apostles with raised hands, bless us also, and fill us with their great joy. You are the one mediator between God and humankind: intercede for us, for our families and for the whole world. Do not let us stand idly looking up, but send us back to pray and to bear witness. Prepare our hearts, with your Mother Mary, for the Spirit whom you have promised, and draw us, your members, to the place where you, our Head, have gone before us. Amen. Alleluia!

kidsaint: Dominic was an Italian boy who studied at the school of St John Bosco. He wanted to be a saint while he was still young. He was kind to the boys others teased, he stopped fights, and he loved to visit Jesus in the church. He died when he was only fourteen. His feast is today, 6 May, but this year the Ascension of Jesus comes first.
2027-05-06.special: THE ASCENSION OF OUR LORD. Sixth Thursday of Resurrection. Day of obligation.
term: The Syriac name of the feast of the Ascension, meaning ‘the going up’; in the West Syriac pronunciation used by the Malankara Church, Suloko. Our Church keeps it on the fortieth day after Easter as a Feast of Our Lord and a day of obligation.

family.explain: Forty days after he rose from the dead, Jesus took his friends to a hill. He lifted up his hands and blessed them, and then he went up into heaven, and a cloud hid him. His friends were not sad! They were full of joy, because they knew Jesus is with the Father and still with them. Jesus promised to send the Holy Spirit, so they went back and prayed with Mary, waiting.
family.intention: We pray that the Holy Spirit will come into our family, and we begin to wait for Pentecost with Mary.
family.ask: Ask: “What can we do together each evening until Pentecost to prepare for the Holy Spirit?”

illus: An old fisherman in Alappuzha used to see off his son each year at Kochi airport when the young man went back to his job abroad. One year his grandson, about six years old, cried as the plane took off. The old man picked him up and said, ‘Don't cry. Your father has gone ahead to make a place ready. Every month he will send what we need, and one day he will bring you there too.’ The boy's mother said later that she thought of that moment every year on the Ascension. Christ has gone ahead, not away. He sends us the gift of the Spirit, and one day he will take us where he is. Like every human picture, it falls short: no plane carries Christ away from us; he is with us always.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, ascended into heaven, lift up your hands over us and bless us, as you blessed your apostles. Fill us with great joy as we gather in your name. Amen. Alleluia!
share: Please let me inherit a double share of your spirit (2 Kings 2:9). What do I ask of the Lord as I prepare for Pentecost?
Why do you stand looking up toward heaven? (Acts 1:11). Where am I passive when the Lord wants me to act?
There is also one mediator between God and humankind (1 Timothy 2:5). For whom do I need to pray today?
They returned to Jerusalem with great joy (Luke 24:52). What gives me joy in this feast?
pm.resp: Christ is ascended into heaven. Alleluia!
interc: For the Church, that she may be the faithful witness of the ascended Lord to the ends of the earth.
For our Major Archbishop, our bishop and all pastors, that they may be clothed with power from on high.
For all in authority in our nation and our state, that they may serve with justice and allow us to lead a quiet and peaceable life.
For our brothers and sisters working abroad and for families separated by distance, that the Lord may keep them.
For our families, that we may prepare with Mary in prayer for the coming of the Holy Spirit.
pm.close: Father, you have raised your Son to your right hand and given him a name above every name. Where he, our Head, has gone, let us his members follow in hope; and send us the Spirit he has promised. Through Christ our Lord. Amen. Alleluia!

homily: Dear friends, forty days after Easter Jesus went up to heaven. Today we celebrate his Ascension, a great Feast of our Lord and a day of obligation.

In the first reading Elijah is taken up to heaven in a chariot of fire. His disciple Elisha would not leave him, and asked for “a double share of your spirit” (2 Kings 2:9). Because Elisha saw his master go, he received his spirit and his mantle. The apostles saw Jesus go up, and ten days later they received the Holy Spirit.

In Acts the apostles ask about the kingdom. Jesus answers, “you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you will be my witnesses... to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8). Then a cloud took him out of their sight, and two angels said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up toward heaven?” (Acts 1:11). The Ascension does not tell us to stare at the sky. It sends us to be witnesses.

Paul tells Timothy that there is “one mediator between God and humankind, Christ Jesus, himself human” (1 Timothy 2:5). A man, our brother, is now at the right hand of the Father, praying for us. That is why we pray for everyone, for rulers, for the sick, for the whole world.

In the Gospel Jesus lifts up his hands and blesses his disciples, and while he is blessing them he is carried up into heaven. And they go back “with great joy” (Luke 24:52). His blessing remains over us.
From tomorrow, with Mary and the apostles, we wait and pray for the Holy Spirit. Let us begin a novena in our homes. Christ has gone ahead to prepare a place for us. Alleluia! Amen.
kids: Children, today Jesus went up to heaven! Before he went, he lifted up his hands and blessed his friends.
He is with his Father, but he is still with us. He promised to send the Holy Spirit. Let us pray with Mary: Come, Holy Spirit!

opts.resolve: This week I will lift up my heart each day to Christ at the Father's right hand and give him one worry.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today we celebrate the Ascension of our Lord. Forty days after Easter, while he was blessing his disciples, he withdrew from them and was carried up into heaven (Luke 24:51). But he did not leave behind the body that was born of Mary and nailed to the Cross. He took our human nature with him into heaven.

Daniel saw in vision one like a human being coming with the clouds of heaven, and to him was given dominion and glory (Daniel 7:13–14). That is the Ascension. A man, our brother, now sits at the right hand of the Father. Hebrews says: we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses. Let us therefore approach the throne of grace with boldness (Hebrews 4:15–16).

The Psalm asks: who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? Lift up your heads, O gates, that the King of glory may come in (Psalm 24:3, 7). Christ has gone in, and he said: in my Father's house there are many dwelling places. I go to prepare a place for you (John 14:2). Heaven is not a dream. It is our home, and the door has been opened by one of us.

So Paul tells us: if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God (Colossians 3:1). That does not mean neglecting the earth. It means living here with our hearts set there. In every Holy Qurbana the priest invites us to lift up our minds on high. Let us really lift them up.

This week let us think a little each day about heaven, our true home. Let us give one worry each day to the Lord at the Father's right hand. And let us live on earth as people whose Head is already in glory. Alleluia! Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Luke tells us what Jesus did just before his Ascension. He said: everything written about me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms must be fulfilled. Then he opened their minds to understand the scriptures (Luke 24:44–45).

Long ago, when Ezra read the book of the law to the people, the Levites gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading (Nehemiah 8:8). Now the risen Lord himself gives the sense of the whole Bible: it speaks of him. Until Pentecost, let us read the Gospel of the day each morning, and ask him to open our minds too.

Then he said: repentance and forgiveness of sins is to be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things (Luke 24:47–48). Jonah preached unwillingly, and yet the people of Nineveh believed God (Jonah 3:5). The apostles would preach willingly, and the Gospel would reach the ends of the earth, even our own Kerala through Mar Thoma.

Finally, while he was blessing them, he was carried up into heaven. And they worshiped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy; and they were continually in the temple blessing God (Luke 24:52–53). The Psalm sings: God has gone up with a shout; sing praises to our King (Psalm 47:5–6). They were not sad. They knew he had not abandoned them, and they waited in praise.

So in these days before Pentecost let us read his word, invite one person back to confession or to the Holy Qurbana, and gather our families for the novena to the Holy Spirit. Let us wait as the apostles waited, with Mary, in joy and in prayer. Alleluia! Amen.
